MorphoHand · real_v1 / SR2 fingertip · contact model overview · 1–9 October 2026 · built 2026-10-09 15:05

Sphere-packed fingertip pads as a distributed contact model for dexterous manipulation in MuJoCo

Covering a fingertip with small MuJoCo contact spheres samples the pressure law of hydroelastic contact, so unmodified MuJoCo reproduces the friction torque and contact area of a soft fingertip. On the two-pad pinch of the real_v1 fingertip and screwdriver, the 1 mm pad slips at Drake hydroelastic’s force to within 0.1 % and starts to spin at a torque 6 % under Drake’s; while it spins, its friction arm is within 1.2 % of the pressure law. The pads agree with Drake to the same degree in CPU MuJoCo, MuJoCo-Warp and Newton. A pad step costs 15 µs on one CPU core, against 1,298 µs for Drake. Under loads below slip the pad creeps 155× faster than Drake.

Terms and metrics

pad
One fingertip’s contact with the tool; is its normal force.
friction arm
Pressure-weighted mean distance of the contact patch from its centre, in mm; a pad turns once the torque about its normal exceeds .
effective
Pull force at slip onset (task 1) divided by ; rigid Coulomb friction gives 1.
creep
Sliding under half the slip load, in µm/s (pull) or °/s (twist); rigid Coulomb friction gives 0.
slip speed
Mean sliding speed in the 50 ms after slip onset, in mm/s.
arm at spin onset
Twist torque at spin onset (task 2) divided by , in mm per pad.
rolling ratio
Tool rotation times its radius over half the pad travel (task 3); rolling without slip gives 1.008.
drift per cycle
Tool displacement per 5 Hz shake cycle below the slip load (task 4), in µm.
swing end
Final tool angle as the pinch force falls from 6 to 0.2 N (task 5); 90° is hanging.
tool turn
Rotation of the tool axis toward vertical in a replayed three-finger turn; within 3° counts replays that end within 3° of Drake’s.
µs per step
Wall time of one 1 ms physics step on one CPU core; per world-step on the GPU.
, , ,
MuJoCo’s solref time constant, solimp impedance and contact inverse inertia, with ; together they set the sphere stiffness, (10).
,
Newton’s hydroelastic stiffness , in N/m³, and its friction gain.
impratio, condim
MuJoCo’s friction-to-normal stiffness ratio; condim 4 adds torsional friction to condim 3.
relaxation time
Drake’s contact dissipation time, 10 ms; a pad sphere’s equivalent is .

Components of a fingertip contact model

The SR2 hand pinches, turns, rolls and releases a 24.5 g screwdriver between two or three soft fingertips. Four contact quantities govern these motions: the normal force with the pad compliance behind it, Coulomb friction in the tangent plane, the friction torque about the contact normal, and the pressure distribution over the contact area, which sets that torque and the centre of pressure. The pinch brake and the wield of arXiv 2609.25619 depend on the friction torque.

The fingertip to be built will probably be printed TPU, possibly with a gyroid infill; its modulus, damping, shear compliance and friction are unmeasured. The model is therefore judged by agreement with pressure-field references and analytic limits on task-level metrics, by consistency across step size and resolution, and by cost. A receding-horizon controller corrects a consistent model error from measured state, provided the model contains the friction torque and slip the task uses.

Contact mechanics of a soft fingertip

1Friction torque of a contact patch

A pad pressed with normal force spreads it over a patch as a pressure . When the tool turns about the contact normal relative to the pad, each area element slides on a circle about the patch centre, and its friction acts at lever :

(1)

is the largest torque the contact transmits before it spins. The friction arm depends on the size of the patch and on the shape of the pressure over it. A point contact has and transmits no torque about its normal, so two point contacts pinching a tool form a free hinge.

2Winkler foundation and the hydroelastic pressure field

A Winkler foundation is a bed of independent springs, each pushing back in proportion to its own compression: , with for a layer of modulus and thickness . Drake’s hydroelastic contact (Elandt et al., 2019) is a foundation of this kind. Each compliant body is given a pressure field that rises with depth below its surface; for a sphere of radius the field is , a Winkler layer with . For a sphere pressed into a flat face, the compression at distance from the patch centre is , the patch is a disc of radius , and

(2)

Eliminating gives the arm as a power of the load:

(3)

For the real_v1 fingertip at Drake’s default  = 10 MPa, a flat face gives . On the 12.5 mm screwdriver the patch is narrower across the tool axis. Integrating the same field over the sphere–cylinder overlap (scripts/hydroelastic_arm_integral.py) gives an arm of 0.820, 0.974 and 1.281 mm at 0.5, 1 and 3 N, with the exponent 1/4 to within 0.1 %. This integral is the reference of the twist task; Drake and the sphere pads are two discretizations of it. The springs are uncoupled, so the pressure is zero outside the geometric overlap.

3Hertz contact

A homogeneous elastic body transmits load sideways through shear, so its surface deflects outside the loaded region and the pressure takes the Hertz form. For a sphere on a rigid flat, with ,

(4)

The two laws differ in how fast the arm grows with load. Between 0.5 and 3 N:

(5)

The ratio is independent of the modulus, so a torque measurement at two loads on a printed fingertip identifies which law the tip follows.

4Lateral coupling: the Pasternak foundation

A Pasternak foundation adds a shear layer that couples neighbouring springs,

(6)

and load spreads a coupling length beyond the overlap. A foundation suffices for ; a coupled foundation is needed for , and a shell or modal model for . Compliant Sphere Lattice Contact (CSLC) is a discrete form of (6): a lattice of spheres tied to the core by anchor springs and to each other by lateral springs. A tangential state per element, which stores shear until it reaches , would add elastic stick before slip; CSLC’s authors describe their model as tangentially stateless. The asides page describes how would be measured on the printed tip (docs/experiments/20261004-codex/20261004-contact_research_asides.html, section on coupled-foundation models).

Sphere-packed pads in MuJoCo

5Sphere discretization of the foundation

The pad replaces the field with spheres of radius whose outer envelope is the fingertip. Each sphere is an ordinary condim 3 MuJoCo contact, and the pad’s force and torque are sums over the spheres in contact:

(7)

Each sphere gets the foundation’s stiffness over its share of the pad. The centres lie on radius , which packs them more densely on the tool than on the fingertip surface:

(8)

The 1 mm pad on a 45° cap has  = 205 spheres of  = 817 N/m. Figure 3 shows the sphere forces sampling the field’s pressure profile at 3 N, and Figure 4 the patches at 3 and 0.5 N. The spacing must be small compared with the patch: at 0.5 N a 2 mm pad touches with 2 spheres and its arm is 13 % long, while the 1 and 0.5 mm pads are within 1 %.

6Static stiffness of a MuJoCo soft contact

MuJoCo solves each step for constraint forces in the space of the contact rows:

(9)

Here is the row acceleration without contact, and the penetration and its rate, the solref, the impedance from solimp, and MuJoCo’s estimate of row ’s inverse inertia. The constrained acceleration is . At rest , so each row satisfies independently, and with a constant impedance

(10)

The coupling through , dense when many spheres press one body, cancels at rest. Each sphere is a spring of stiffness regardless of how many neighbours touch, so in statics the pad is a discrete Winkler foundation. Codex’s static audit measured the force per overlap equal to (10) to floating-point precision (docs/experiments/20261004-codex/20261004-distributed_contact.html). Solving (10) for the impedance gives , which is positive only for : 5.1 ms for the 1 mm pad and 10.2 ms for the 0.5 mm pad, so a softer sphere needs a longer time constant. The 1 mm pad uses  = 10 ms ( = 0.741) and relaxes in  = 20 ms, twice Drake’s 10 ms on the bed; the slip force and the friction arm are measured in quasi-static ramps and do not depend on it.

7Inverse-inertia calibration

is the sum of the two bodies’ inverse weights, so by (10) a sphere’s stiffness depends on the mass behind the contact. Calibrated with the nominal tool and reused for a tool four times heavier, each sphere comes out 2.83× too stiff, and for a tool four times lighter 0.28×. Computing from the compiled model for each pad–object pair at load, and from it, removes the dependence at no run-time cost. In MuJoCo 3.6 is the sum of the bodies’ body_invweight0, which is independent of pose, so the load-time value is exact. With it the arm is 0.802 mm at 0.5 N and 1.246 mm at 3 N for all three masses, 2 and 3 % under the hydroelastic law; with the fixed value it moves by +37 and −23 % (Figure 5). The chain’s plant already calibrates each trial this way, so the per-step remapping of every contact that Codex built is unnecessary. The friction arm depends on the stiffness only through the patch radius:

(11)

The same factor sets the stiffness of every MuJoCo contact, not only of the pads: solref is a spring on the constraint acceleration, so a contact realises its solref stiffness times the effective mass as a force stiffness, and the pads’ divides that mass out. Newton’s hydroelastic contact passes each patch point to MuJoCo-Warp with a force stiffness and writes it as without the factor, so on the bed ( = 17.4 g) it sank 7.1–7.4 times as deep as Drake. Multiplying its by the inverse-weight sum of the solver’s own MuJoCo model, , gives 1.02–1.04 times Drake’s sink with no parameter fitted (docs/experiments/20261006-hom_turn3/20261006-servo_refit_hom_turn_pad_cost.html, Section 4). The pads carry into Newton’s point-contact pipeline with two settings: recomputed from the inverse weights of Newton’s MuJoCo model, which gives the bed’s railed pads 16.7 1/kg against the MJCF compile’s 50 ( 0.866 → 0.788), and a friction gain for which SolverMuJoCo’s friction-row time constant equals the pads’ (4.4 on the bed). With Newton’s default the friction rows get  s and the braked tool swung to 108°; with it swings to 88.3°, as in MuJoCo.

8Creep under MuJoCo’s soft friction

Creep is the steady sliding of a contact under a tangential load below its friction limit; rigid Coulomb friction gives none. A sphere’s friction rows enter (9) with and no position term, and with a regulariser set by impratio . At zero acceleration (9) gives , a constant sliding speed. With rows sharing a load ,

(12)

For the 1 mm pad ( = 0.741,  = 10 ms,  = 100) held at half its slip force in bed task 1, (12) gives 0.5 N: 0.019 predicted, 0.023 mm/s measured (16 spheres); 1 N: 0.028 predicted, 0.031 mm/s measured (22 spheres); 3 N: 0.044 predicted, 0.053 mm/s measured (42 spheres). Drake’s SAP solver holds the same load with about 177× less creep (0.1–0.3 µm/s), so creep is the largest disagreement between MuJoCo and the references in the bed. Raising impratio from 100 to 1000 cuts the median creep of bed task 6 from 16.8 to 1.0 µm/s; ten noslip_iterations take it to -0.54 µm/s.

9Step-size bound for a pad

Away from rest, the rows of one pad move together. For rows of equal on one body, has the eigenvalue along their common motion, so (9) gives that motion an effective impedance and a damping rate :

(13)

MuJoCo evaluates with the velocity at the start of the step, so the damping is explicit and stable for :

(14)

For the 1 mm pads ( = 0.74–0.89,  = 10–15 ms) the bound is 7–13 ms, and it cannot fall as more spheres touch because . The pads gave the same task results from 50 µs to 10 ms steps in Codex’s 50 Hz sweep (Figure 8). Codex’s per-contact mapping set to impose each sphere’s spring and damper exactly. Then , and the summed contact damping , with  = 24.5 N·s/m per sphere, requires : 60–90 µs for 20–30 spheres. Those runs diverged at every step from 0.5 to 10 ms and completed only at 50 µs. MuJoCo applies its clamp per row, which leaves this collective mode unbounded. Bed task 7 holds the tool against gravity at 1 N per pad for 1 s with from 0.2 to 0.95, of 5, 10 and 20 ms and steps from 0.25 to 15 ms, with MuJoCo’s clamp switched off so that stays as set. In the other 2,  = 0.9 and 0.95 at  = 20 ms, the tool is ejected at 15 ms, below bounds of 18–19 ms. With the clamp on, as MuJoCo runs by default, the pads with  ≥ 0.5 hold at every step up to 10 ms at all three , and those with 0.2 and 0.35 fail from 2 to 10 ms, where the clamped bound falls below .

10condim 4 with a rescheduled torsional coefficient

condim 4 keeps one contact per pad and adds a torsional coefficient , bounded with the tangential force in an elliptic cone . Matching (3) requires , which varies with load, so the plant rewrites it before every step from the last normal force:

(15)

The bed’s condim 4 takes and the exponent from a fit to Drake’s torque on this rig (, 0.2498), so it reproduces Drake’s torque by construction, at the cost of one coefficient write per contact per step. With a single contact point, its centre of pressure is fixed, and under a pure pull or roll it behaves as condim 3. The chain page derives the brake that uses it (docs/experiments/20261002-hom_chain/20261002-hom_screwdriver_chain.html, steps 3 and 5).

Reference models

Drake hydroelastic

Drake gives each compliant body a pressure field on a tetrahedral mesh, for the fingertip sphere at a 1 mm resolution, and computes the contact surface as the rigid tool’s surface inside it. Each face has a pressure, and the SAP solver integrates force and friction over the faces with a convex, regularised friction law; under a held load it creeps about 100× less than MuJoCo’s soft friction rows. It is the reference for every task on these pages and costs 1–2 ms per step on one core. Importing the hand from MJCF needs the model’s contact exclusions applied as collision filters; without them the distal links locked against their own yaw links (chain page).

Newton hydroelastic

Newton (commit 009158e6) represents each shape by a sparse signed-distance grid, extracts the patch where the two shapes’ pressures balance by marching cubes, and hands each triangle to the solver as a contact point with its own stiffness. An optional reduction merges them into a few representative contacts. Friction stays per point in the MuJoCo-Warp or XPBD solver, so the friction torque comes from the spread of the points, as with the sphere pads. Codex’s static check on the SR2 pinch put the torque capacity within 1–6 % of the continuum at 0.25 mm voxels without reduction; reduction lowered it by 16–25 % and 1 mm voxels by up to 69 %. Newton’s MJCF importer stores a one-value default solref with damping ratio 0, and contacts with zero Newton stiffness fall back to it, so the bed and hand scenes are imported with two-value solrefs. SolverMuJoCo realises each contact’s stiffness times the effective mass, so the bed’s pads sank 7.1–7.4 times as deep as Drake; with divided by (step 7) they sink 1.02–1.04 times Drake’s depth and start to spin at 0.76–0.88 of Drake’s onset torque. One GPU world costs 0.5 ms per step with reduction and 1.5 ms without. On the bed, all faces at 0.5 mm voxels give the pressure law’s friction arm at 0.5 and 1 N and the reduced contacts 0.77–0.88 of it, and friction rows of 10 ms or longer stop the braked tool at hanging where the default 3.9 ms swings it to 130° (docs/experiments/20261007-newton_hydro_tests/).

Compliant Sphere Lattice Contact

CSLC represents the fingertip surface by a lattice of spheres tied to the rigid core by anchor springs and to their neighbours by lateral springs, and solves the lattice for quasi-static equilibrium against the object with warm-started damped Jacobi iterations. Its presliding friction saturates smoothly, and its authors describe the model as tangentially stateless, without kinetic sliding dynamics. It was not run here; its paper is in docs/experiments/20261004-codex/22_Compliant_Sphere_Lattice_Co.pdf.

Comparison with the reference models

The comparison bed runs five tasks on the two-pad rig of the 10-01 study at 1 and 5 ms steps (759 cases). Pull and twist load the pinch until the tool slides or spins; roll moves one pad so the tool rolls between them; shake drives the held tool at 5 Hz under gravity; brake lowers the pinch force until the tool swings toward hanging. Shading compares each model with Drake hydroelastic: within 10 % (dark), 10–25 % (light), 25–50 % (amber), beyond 50 % or a failed case (red). A dash marks a case not run.

Twist. Drake’s arm at the onset of spin is 0.839, 0.987, 1.275 mm at 0.5, 1 and 3 N, within 2.5 % of the integrated law (3); the 1 mm pad gives 0.787, 0.924, 1.193 mm, 3.9–6.9 % below it. Once every sphere slides, the pad’s arm is within 1.2 % of the law and Drake’s 2.2–2.7 % above it. The pad’s shortfall appears only at onset, where the tool turns 1.4–2.0° before it spins (Drake 0.02–0.03°), which points to MuJoCo’s soft friction rows rather than the pressure law. Both arms grow by 1.52 between 0.5 and 3 N, close to the foundation ratio of 1.565; Hertz gives 1.82 (Figure 2). condim 4, whose follows the fit to Drake’s torque (step 10), is 5.1–8.1 % above the law at onset and 2.2–2.3 % above it while sliding. Held at half the onset torque, the pad turns at 1.1–1.6 °/s and Drake at 0.01 °/s.

Brake. Lowering the pinch from 6 to 0.2 N over 4 s swings the tool to 87.3° in Drake, 88.3° with the 1 mm pad and 87.5° with condim 4, with peak rates of 293, 263 and 257 °/s. Point contact swings through to 175° and slides 27 mm along the tool.

Shake. At 0.5 N and 2 g the load stays below the rigid-Coulomb slip threshold, so the drift is creep: 2.3 µm per cycle with the pad against 0.02 µm in Drake.

Roll. Moving one pad 10 mm along the tool at 10 mm/s rolls the tool between the pads in every model, at 0.5 to 3 N and both steps. At 1 N the rolling ratio is 1.0078 (Drake hydroelastic), 1.0116 (MuJoCo 1 mm sphere pad), 1.0121 (MuJoCo point contact, condim 3), 1.0121 (MuJoCo condim 4, rescheduled), 1.0079 (Newton hydroelastic, ); no-slip rolling between the spheres gives 1.0082. The differences follow the depth of the contact point: the pad’s lies 0.09 mm inside the tool surface and Drake’s 0.02 mm, and a contact at a smaller radius turns the tool further for the same travel. The contacts slip at most 33 µm over 5 mm of rolling, and no model loses the tool.

Agreement of the pads with Drake across MuJoCo, MuJoCo-Warp and Newton

The pads are the same contact model in CPU MuJoCo, MuJoCo-Warp and Newton’s point-contact pipeline once Newton gets the solver’s inverse weights (step 7). MuJoCo-Warp ports MuJoCo’s constraint solver to the GPU and Newton’s SolverMuJoCo runs MuJoCo-Warp, so the three are one solver in three implementations; Newton’s hydroelastic contact and Drake are the independent comparisons. Figure 7 compares the three, Newton’s mass-corrected hydroelastic contact on the plain block and MuJoCo point contact with Drake on the bed’s twist and brake and on the open-loop plan replay of the three-finger turn on the eight deployed hands (working servo plant, , 24 placements paired with Drake by hand and placement). The three pad implementations agree with Drake to the same degree: onset torque 0.94 of Drake’s at 0.5–3 N, largest swing within 1.1° of Drake’s 87.3°, the turn within 3° of Drake on 23, 23 and 22 of 24 placements, every one of the 40 placements held in all three, and grip force 0.98–1.53 of Drake’s. The mass-corrected hydroelastic contact reaches 0.76–0.88 of Drake’s onset torque but swings the braked tool to 130° and turns within 3° on 7 of 24; point contact holds every placement of the turn but transmits 0.05–0.16 of the onset torque and lets the braked tool spin out of the pinch (docs/experiments/20261006-hom_turn3/20261006-servo_refit_hom_turn_pad_cost.html, Section 5).

The pads also carry learned behaviour between implementations. The D6 reorientation trained from scratch in MuJoCo-Warp for 20 M steps holds the tool in 64 and 64 of 64 deterministic rollouts with the 1 mm pads (final cosine with vertical 0.43–0.44). Replayed open loop from the reorientation onset in CPU MuJoCo, the pad policies end within 0.02 in cosine of MuJoCo-Warp with the tool held; the policies trained on the TPU block as one convex mesh lose the tool in CPU MuJoCo within 0.3 s. Films of the four policies and the replays in Drake and Newton: docs/experiments/20261006-hom_turn3/20261006-servo_refit_hom_turn_pad_cost.html, Section 6. Trained for 40 M steps on four fingertip contact models, the D6 reorientation policies on the 1 mm pads and on the pads mounted on a sprung skin (5 policies) keep the tool in 216 of 220 open-loop replays of their finger targets in CPU MuJoCo, Drake and Newton, and the 3 policies trained with point contact on the box tip or the TPU block in 3 of 132. Closed loop in MuJoCo-Warp under the other contact models of the TPU block, the skin policies hold 99 % of the rollouts, the pad policies 76 % and the TPU-mesh policies 51 %; pad and skin training cost 1.7× and 2.3× the TPU mesh’s time per iteration: docs/experiments/20261008-contact_model_policies/20261008-fingertip_contact_model_policies.html. The same 1 mm pads carry the hand–object scale landscape of the SR2 hand (17 finger-base layouts × 18 cylinders and spheres, grasp robustness and the three-finger turn), where point contact on the TPU block ranks the layouts nearly as the pads do: docs/experiments/20261008-hand_object_scale/20261008-finger_spacing_object_size.html.

Consistency across step size

Codex ran the paper’s Exp 2 twist sequence with a 20 ms controller and physics steps from 50 µs to 10 ms. The 1 mm pad ends the sequence at −48.3 to −44.9° about the pinch axis over all six steps, Drake hydroelastic at −49.0 to −48.8°. Both include the same ratchet toward hanging that the chain page traced to free pad spin. The four per-contact mappings diverged in 20 of 24 runs, every step from 0.5 ms up, and the 4 that finished at 50 µs ended at −67 to −56°. At equal step the pad costs 45× less than Drake at 1 ms and 23× less at 10 ms (Figure 8).

Cost

The cost of one physics step at 1 ms. On one CPU core, on the bed rig in task 1: MuJoCo point contact, condim 3, 3.2 µs; MuJoCo condim 4, rescheduled, 10.6 µs; MuJoCo 1 mm sphere pad, 15.1 µs; Drake hydroelastic, 1,298 µs. One world alone on the GPU, on the SR2 holding fixture of Figure 10 with each 10-step block captured as a CUDA graph: MuJoCo-Warp 1 mm sphere pad, 341 µs; Newton 1 mm sphere pad, 313 µs; Newton hydroelastic, , 425 µs. A single GPU world is bound by kernel launches. In a batch on the same fixture the cost per world-step at the batch of highest throughput (Figure 10) is 1.08 µs for the MuJoCo-Warp 1 mm sphere pad (4,096 worlds), 1.19 µs for the Newton 1 mm sphere pad (2,048 worlds), 1.85 µs for the Newton hydroelastic tip, (4,096 worlds). Figure 9 plots both costs against each model’s deviation from Drake over the metrics of Table 2. On one held state of the D6 RL env at 1,024 and 2,048 worlds (the trainer’s 2 ms step), MuJoCo-Warp steps the 1 mm pads in 2.2–2.4 µs of physics per world-step, the TPU block as one mesh in 1.0–1.6 µs and Newton’s mass-corrected hydroelastic block in 4.2–4.3 µs; the RL env with the pads runs 12 % fewer env steps per second than with the box tip at 2,048 envs, because physics is about a tenth of an env step.

The whole task

The chain page runs the controller of arXiv 2609.25619 through pick, braked swing, squeeze and peg-hole insertion on the SR2 hand in eight contact models, and the paper’s Exp 2, Exp 3 and wield with the sphere pads. The closed-loop brake ends the swing at 91.3° in Drake hydroelastic and 90.5° with the 1 mm pad, and both insert the tool; point contact drops it. The films below are from that page (docs/experiments/20261002-hom_chain/20261002-hom_screwdriver_chain.html, artifact).

Future work

  • Hertz or foundation on the printed tip. Measure the friction torque of the printed fingertip on the screwdriver at 0.5 and 3 N (torque sensor under a fixed pinch, slow spin). A ratio near 1.57 keeps a foundation model; near 1.82 calls for lateral coupling, equation (5).
  • Coupling length of the TPU print. Indent the print at one point and map the surface displacement around it; fit and compare with the 1.6–2.5 mm patch radius (asides page).
  • Creep in the whole task. Re-run the chain’s hold and the wield with impratio 1000, the setting at which bed task 6 brings the pad’s creep toward Drake’s (step 8), and record the cost per step.
  • Newton’s braked swing. With friction rows of 10 ms Newton’s hydroelastic tip stops the braked tool at hanging but lets it fall through 80° at 1.2–1.3 N, where Drake passes 80° at 0.39 N, and a 10–25 % shorter arm does not reproduce that in condim 4. Log the torque of Newton’s contact forces about the pinch axis during the fall (2026-10-07 Newton page, open items).
  • The modulus. Every model here uses Drake’s default  MPa. The arm scales as , so a TPU tip at 2–5 MPa lengthens it by 19–50 %; refit once the tip is measured.
  • Pre-slip shear. The pads and Drake store no elastic tangential displacement. Mounting the spheres on a child body with spring-loaded tangential slides and a normal hinge gives Mindlin’s presliding at 1.3× the pads’ GPU cost and keeps the bed’s pull and brake results and the twist onset to 1 N; ball joints under the spheres add Mindlin’s hysteresis at 27× (docs/experiments/20261007-native_compliance/). A slow tangential load cycle on the printed tip (hysteresis loop below the slip force) measures whether the tip needs either.

Drake and the spheres integrate the same pressure law, which is local and has no state. Neither represents shear compliance before slip, hysteresis or the lateral spread of load in an elastic tip, and both give a contact radius growing as ; measured soft fingertips give exponents from 0 to 1/3, depending on the material (Xydas and Kao). The spheres add the creep of MuJoCo’s soft friction rows and miss surface features finer than their 1 mm spacing.
